tldr: By pretraining an action decoder using large-scale privileged reinforcement learning in simulation and freezing it during downstream adaptation, the proposed method maps visual features directly to latent task context, enabling precise and robust dexterous manipulation from only a handful of visual demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed Latent RL Prior framework. (a) Privileged pretraining: latent task context is extracted from ground-truth object and goal states via a Q-Former and distilled into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and diffusion time. (b) Visual adaptation: the action decoder is kept completely frozen while only the image encoder and visual Q-Former are trained using action supervision alone. For bimanual tasks, both arms share the identical action decoder to acquire coordinated behaviors.
overview:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is one of the most challenging areas in robotics, as contact states and object dynamics shift rapidly. When attempting imitation learning from camera images and a small number of demonstrations, acquiring both visual scene understanding and millimeter-precision fingertip control from scratch simultaneously is extremely difficult. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation leveraging abundant "privileged information"—such as 3D object positions and target poses—can already discover sophisticated fingertip control skills. However, privileged information is unavailable during real-world deployment, making the reuse of this acquired control knowledge a major challenge.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed "Latent RL Prior," a framework that preserves control skills learned via privileged RL inside an action generation model and connects visual inputs directly to its latent representation. First, behaviors of an RL agent trained on large-scale pose alignment tasks in simulation are distilled into a flow-matching action decoder. When adapting to downstream visual tasks, this capable action decoder is completely frozen, and only a visual interface that translates image features into latent task context is trained using action prediction loss. This requires no privileged labels or latent targets at all, adapting purely with standard visual imitation learning data. Furthermore, by sharing the same single-arm decoder across both arms, the framework naturally scales to bimanual coordinated manipulation.

Experiments evaluated three tasks: pose alignment with unseen objects, door lifting, and bimanual assembly. The results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art foundation models like $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 in low-data regimes. On door lifting and bimanual assembly, it exceeded the success rates of full-data baselines while using $10\times$ and $5\times$ fewer demonstrations, respectively. Analysis also confirmed that the robustness to mass variations and contact-force representations acquired during pretraining are strongly retained in downstream tasks.
contributions: Proposed Latent RL Prior, a visual adaptation framework trained via action supervision alone that keeps an action decoder pretrained with privileged RL frozen and directly conditions it on latent context from visual inputs.

Demonstrated an extension to bimanual manipulation where a single pretrained single-arm action decoder is shared across both arms, achieving coordinated two-arm behaviors using only self-attention within the visual Q-Former.

Showed substantially superior demonstration efficiency across three dexterous manipulation tasks compared to state-of-the-art VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, GR00T N1.7) and training from scratch (up to $10\times$ data efficiency).
Revealed through analysis that the visually adapted model preserves robustness to unseen mass variations and exhibits high linear decodability of contact-force information.

sections.heading: Turning Control Skills from Simulated RL into a Prior for Visual Imitation Learning
sections.summary: Learning dexterous multi-fingered manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is difficult, but large-scale RL in simulation acquires rich control skills. This work introduces Latent RL Prior, which pretrains an action decoder from privileged RL and learns a visual interface to its latent representation, achieving high data efficiency on downstream tasks.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands requires fine-grained coordination between arms and fingers under constantly changing contact states and object dynamics. However, attempting to learn these behaviors from a small number of visual demonstrations creates a steep hurdle: policies must acquire both perceptual grounding of visual information and precise control generation simultaneously.

Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pretrained on diverse robotic datasets and vision-language corpora have attracted significant attention. This paper focuses on a complementary source of control skills: large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation. In simulation, one has access to privileged information such as ground-truth meshes, mass properties, and target poses, making it possible to train sophisticated control policies that generalize across diverse shapes and physical dynamics. However, this privileged information is absent in real deployment environments. Many existing approaches have relied on intermediate workarounds, such as training explicit object pose estimators for deployment.

The core hypothesis of this research is that freezing and preserving the pretrained pathways for proprioception processing and action generation can drastically cut down the amount of visual demonstration data needed for downstream task adaptation. The proposed Latent RL Prior freezes a flow-matching action decoder distilled from privileged RL and trains only a converter from images to latent task context. This opens a path to adapting to new tasks with minimal visual demonstrations without needing any privileged supervision labels.

sections.heading: Positioning Within Privileged RL Distillation and the Lineage of VLA Models
sections.summary: This work lies at the intersection of dexterous manipulation via RL, policy transfer with privileged information, and visual imitation learning / VLA models. Unlike conventional adaptation methods, it trains the visual interface purely through downstream action loss, without requiring privileged labels or paired latent representations.
sections.details:
### Dexterous Manipulation via Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement learning with dynamics randomization has enabled challenging dexterous manipulation skills, such as in-hand object rotation. In particular, recent advances in massively parallel simulators have unlocked scalable learning through extensive interaction. For example, prior work SimToolReal trains a single RL teacher policy that aligns procedurally generated objects of varied geometries to target poses. This paper distills rollouts from this teacher model into an action decoder, using it as a foundation to reuse control priors for downstream tasks.

### Transfer Methods Using Privileged Information
Techniques for training observation-restricted policies using privileged information include asymmetric actor-critic setups and policy distillation such as "Learning by Cheating." Approaches like Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) have also been proposed to infer privileged latent representations from observation history. However, these methods typically require matching losses against privileged latent targets in the downstream environment. In contrast, visual adaptation in this work relies solely on action supervision from downstream demonstrations, without using any privileged labels or pretrained latent targets.

### Visual Imitation Learning and Generalist Robot Policies
Diffusion-based action generation frameworks, including Action Chunking and flow matching, have demonstrated strong results in learning from visual demonstrations. In addition, VLA models such as $\pi_0$ and GR00T integrate pretrained vision-language representations with action heads. The proposed approach combines strong visual representations from DINOv2 with precise control priors distilled from privileged RL, demonstrating superior adaptation efficiency in low-data regimes compared to full-parameter fine-tuning of existing models.

sections.heading: A Two-Stage Approach: Freezing the Privileged RL Action Decoder and Bridging Latents via Visual Q-Former
sections.summary: The method consists of two stages: privileged pretraining, which distills privileged RL rollouts into an action decoder, and visual adaptation, which freezes the decoder and learns latent context from images. By sharing the single-arm decoder and coordinating queries via self-attention in the Q-Former, it naturally extends to bimanual tasks.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
At time $t$, the robot receives a proprioceptive history $\mathcal{R}_t$ (such as joint positions and velocities) and an image history $\mathcal{I}_t$ from multiple cameras, predicting an action chunk $\mathcal{A}_t$ over the next $K$ steps. The framework represents task information using $M$ latent context tokens ${\bm{Z}}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d}$, which are fed into the action decoder alongside the proprioceptive history $\mathcal{R}_t$. During pretraining, ${\bm{Z}}_t$ is generated from privileged history $\mathcal{P}_t$, whereas during downstream visual adaptation, ${\bm{Z}}_t$ is generated from image history $\mathcal{I}_t$.

### 3.2 Privileged Pretraining
Following the SimToolReal setup, the authors collect a dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RL}}$ of 100,000 successful rollouts from an RL teacher policy trained to align objects with randomized shapes, sizes, and densities into target poses.
This privileged history is passed through a state tokenizer $T_\eta$ and a Q-Former $Q_\psi$ to produce latent context ${\bm{Z}}_t$. The action decoder $v_\theta$ uses a Transformer architecture where action tokens cross-attend to the latent context tokens. Crucially, the proprioceptive history $\mathcal{R}_t$ and flow-matching time step $\tau$ are injected into each block via Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN). This decoupled pathway ensures that even when the context source shifts to visual inputs downstream, core proprioceptive processing and action generation capabilities remain fully intact.

### 3.3 Visual Adaptation
In the visual adaptation stage, the pretrained action decoder $v_\theta$ is completely frozen. A DINOv2-based image encoder $E_{\mathrm{vis}}$ and visual Q-Former $Q_\phi$ are introduced to predict the decoder's latent context ${\bm{Z}}_t^{\mathrm{latent}}$ directly from visual features (Latent Transfer). Training uses only flow-matching loss over the downstream demonstration dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{vis}}$, requiring zero privileged information or latent targets.
For comparison, an "Explicit Transfer" baseline is also formulated, which decodes privileged states (such as object poses) from images and feeds them into the pretrained state encoder.

### Extension to Multi-Arm Manipulation
For bimanual tasks, rather than training separate action decoders for each arm, the single pretrained single-arm decoder $v_\theta$ is shared across both arms (weight sharing). The visual Q-Former initializes $M$ queries for the left arm and $M$ queries for the right arm, allowing cross-arm communication via self-attention across all queries. The resulting coordinated latent contexts ${\bm{Z}}_t^L, {\bm{Z}}_t^R$ are fed into the identical decoder along with each arm's respective proprioception, achieving coordinated bimanual control while capitalizing on single-arm control skills.

captions.F1: Overall architecture of Latent RL Prior. (a) Privileged pretraining pipeline, distilling privileged information into the action decoder via a Q-Former. (b) Visual adaptation pipeline, keeping the action decoder frozen while a visual Q-Former generates latent context tokens directly from images. In bimanual setups, left and right arm queries interact through self-attention within the same Q-Former.

sections.heading: Outperforming VLA Baselines in Data Efficiency and Retaining Physical Control Capabilities
sections.summary: Evaluations across three simulation tasks (unseen brush alignment, door lifting, and bimanual assembly) show that the proposed method surpasses the full-data performance of $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 using 5 to 10 times fewer demonstrations. Robustness to unseen mass variations and retention of contact-force representations were also verified.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted in MuJoCo Warp using KUKA iiwa arms equipped with SHARPA multi-fingered hands. The pretraining task involved aligning diverse procedurally generated objects, while downstream evaluations covered three tasks:
- **Target pose alignment**: Grasping an unseen blue brush and aligning it to a target pose (evaluated under strict $\epsilon=0.015$ m and loose $\epsilon=0.05$ m thresholds).
- **Door lifting**: Lifting a door with randomized height and position to expose a cube behind it.
- **Bimanual assembly**: Holding separate parts in each hand, reorienting them in-hand, and inserting a peg into a hole.

Baselines included full-parameter fine-tuning of state-of-the-art VLA models $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7, as well as a Scratch model that trains the identical architecture from scratch without the pretrained prior.

### 4.2 Visual Demonstration Efficiency
The proposed method significantly outperformed VLA baselines across all evaluated tasks, with the advantage being especially pronounced in low-data regimes. In door lifting, the proposed method achieved higher success rates with only 50 demonstrations than $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 achieved with 500 demonstrations (the full dataset), demonstrating a $10\times$ data efficiency improvement. In bimanual assembly, it surpassed the performance of both baselines trained on 5,000 demonstrations using just 1,000 demonstrations ($5\times$ data efficiency).
Comparisons with the Scratch model (Figure F5) also showed substantial performance gains, confirming that high data efficiency stems from the frozen RL action decoder rather than the visual encoder alone.

### 4.3 Latent Transfer vs. Explicit Transfer
Comparing Latent Transfer (direct mapping to latent space) against Explicit Transfer (predicting privileged states explicitly before passing them to the state encoder) showed that Latent Transfer yielded consistently higher success rates and superior training stability. Routing visual predictions through an explicit intermediate state prediction led to higher training variance, whereas direct latent conditioning proved far better suited for optimization via action loss.

### 4.4 Ablation Studies
Investigating learning rates for the image encoder and action decoder revealed that applying a conservative update (small learning rate) to the image encoder while completely freezing the action decoder achieved the highest accuracy, especially under the strict threshold. Fine-tuning the action decoder on small demonstration sets caused overfitting and degraded the general-purpose control skills acquired during pretraining.

### 4.5 Retention of Control Behavior and Physical Information
The authors investigated how well the visually adapted model retained physical capabilities from RL pretraining.
- **Generalization to Mass Variations**: Although visual demonstrations featured only a single mass, increasing object mass during evaluation caused $\pi_{0.5}$'s performance to drop sharply, whereas the proposed method remained robust (at 5.0 kg in door lifting, $\pi_{0.5}$ achieved 12.9% success while the proposed method maintained 32.6%).
- **Linear Probing of Contact Forces**: Fitting a linear ridge regression to intermediate features of the frozen decoder to predict contact forces yielded significantly higher accuracy (lower RMSE) than the Scratch model. A model adapted with only 200 demonstrations captured contact forces more accurately than a model trained from scratch on 4,000 demonstrations, providing strong evidence that RL-acquired contact-control knowledge is preserved inside the decoder.

sections.heading: Limitations: Simulation Dependence and Fixed Robot Morphology
sections.summary: While the framework improves downstream visual data efficiency, pretraining requires large-scale simulation and a high-performing privileged RL teacher. Furthermore, evaluations are restricted to simulation, and the setup does not accommodate changes in robot morphology.
sections.details:
The claims in this paper specifically center on "visual demonstration efficiency in downstream tasks," rather than total computation or data efficiency including pretraining. The method relies on a high-quality privileged RL teacher and extensive interaction experience in simulation. In addition, because the action decoder is frozen for reuse, it risks inheriting failure modes from the teacher policy or struggling with tasks requiring fundamentally different control dynamics.

Furthermore, all evaluations were conducted on a single robot configuration (KUKA iiwa + SHARPA hand). While the single-arm decoder successfully scaled to bimanual tasks, transfer across differing robot arm or hand morphologies was not evaluated. Because demonstration collection and evaluation were carried out entirely within simulation, Sim-to-Real transfer and real-world robot deployment remain important open directions for future work.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Powerful Paradigm of Freezing Control Knowledge and Rewiring Visual Interfaces
sections.summary: Freezing control priors learned through privileged RL and wiring visual inputs directly into their latent context enables dexterous manipulation with remarkable data efficiency. In an era dominated by foundation models, this provides significant evidence for the enduring value of control priors derived from simulated RL.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Latent RL Prior, extracting control knowledge acquired through large-scale privileged reinforcement learning in simulation into a flow-matching action decoder and keeping it frozen while learning visual latent context for adaptation. Using simple action prediction loss without privileged supervision, the method substantially surpassed state-of-the-art VLA models in data efficiency, achieving a $10\times$ demonstration reduction on door lifting and a $5\times$ reduction on bimanual assembly.

Experiments further confirmed that direct latent bridging outperforms explicit state prediction, and freezing the action decoder retains robustness to mass variations and contact-force representations. Moving beyond relying solely on large-scale vision-language pretraining (VLAs), reusing physical simulation experience as an action-decoder prior represents a highly promising direction for data-efficient robot learning.

takeaways: For acquiring dexterous fingertip control, freezing and reusing an action decoder trained via privileged RL in simulation as a prior is far more data-efficient than fine-tuning generalist VLA models.

When interfacing vision with a controller, mapping visual features directly into latent context (e.g., via a Q-Former) yields higher performance and greater training stability than explicitly estimating privileged states (like object poses).

When downstream demonstrations are scarce, keeping the pretrained action decoder completely frozen while applying conservative updates to the vision encoder is essential to prevent overfitting and preserve control priors.
Decoders pretrained with dynamics randomization in RL retain robust internal representations of contact forces and generalize to unseen mass variations even after downstream visual adaptation.
limitations: While downstream demo efficiency is high, pretraining requires massive numbers of simulated interaction steps and the engineering of a high-performing privileged RL teacher model.
The approach is tied to the specific robot morphology (arm and multi-fingered hand) used during pretraining, without zero-shot transfer capabilities across different hardware configurations.

All validations were conducted entirely within a simulated environment (MuJoCo Warp); performance under real-world visual domain gaps and physical dynamics mismatches (Sim-to-Real) has not yet been verified.
